newsitem.title: USA: US bonds close higher after erasing early losses - May 15.
newsitem.headline: US bonds close higher after erasing early losses - May 15.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended higher on Thursday after early losses were erased and late short-covering lifted prices to session highs.

Prices fell near the outset of the trading session when the government said new jobless claims had dropped sharply in the latest week and that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) without its more volatile food and energy components had risen 0.3 percent in April. The market had expected a smaller, 0.2 percent increase in the so-called core CPI.
The total CPI rose 0.1 percent, as expected.

The market began to trim its steepest losses after the Federal Reserve reported that U.S. industrial production was flat in April and that the portion of the nation's mines, utilities and factories employed in that production slipped to 83.4 percent from a downwardly revised 83.7 percent. The Fed also trimmed its previous measure of March industrial output to 0.6 percent from the 0.9 percent it first reported.
Economists said the industrial production data showed that the economy was growing moderately but that there was a little less pressure on capacity than had been previously thought.
The industrial production report was soon followed by another piece of data that the bond market found soothing.
The Philadelphia Federal Reserve reported that its index of area business conditions fell in May from its April level. On that news, bonds erased the bulk of their remaining losses.
The dollar's recovery to about 116 yen from 114.70 yen hit overnight in European trading also bouyed bond prices.

"The market went down on the CPI, but most important was the industrial production data," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "That report pulled the market off its lows."
Talk of the Fed buying bonds and central bank purchases of two- and five-year notes was also positive and encouraged some short-covering, analysts said.

"We're coming to the end of this stream of data," said David Jones, vice chairman and chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "April industrial production was depressed by strikes in the auto industry (against General Motors and Chrysler) but the pattern of data in general confirms in my mind that there will be no (Federal Reserve interest rate) tightening at the May 20 (monetary policy) meeting."
Jones said the data released this week that supported the notion of no Fed tightening included the 0.3 percent drop in April retail sales and a 0.6 percent drop in the April Producer Price Index.

Jones said he estimated the annual rate of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth would slow from 5.6 percent in the first quarter to 2.5 percent in the second quarter, pick up to three percent in the third quarter and 3.5 percent in the fourth.
Alexy and Jones said the market was unlikely to move out of its current range before the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday.
"I guess we just kind of sit here until we get the news from the Fed," said Jones.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 96-30/32, up 7/32 to yield 6.87 percent. The 10-year Treasury note closed aat 99-24/32, up 3/32 to yield 6.66 percent. Five-year notes ended at 100-15/32, up 2/32 to yield 6.51 percent.
Near the shorter end of the maturity range, two-year notes closed at 100-9/32, up 1/32 to yield 6.22 percent.
Six-month and year-bill rates each slipped one basis point to 5.28 percent and 4.98 percent, respectively. Three-month bill rates dropped five basis points to 4.98 percent.
